sources.title: Search snippet only: Old Indian / Chigorin Indian results (Wikipedia Chigorin pages and others)

overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.

white_ideas.idea: Occupy the centre with pawns and pieces (e4 and Nf3), keeping the space advantage.
Main line Ukrainian: 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, with a slight edge.
Maintain central tension and restrict Black's ...e5 break or meet it favourably.

black_ideas.idea: Establish a solid pawn structure with ...d6 and ...e5, pieces behind it.
Develop the bishop modestly to e7 and castle, rather than fianchetto; a Philidor-like structure.
Typical follow-ups named in the search snippet: ...c6, ...a5, ...Na6, ...f6 (the snippet also lists '...Kd8-c7', which looks like a typo for ...Qc7).
Janowski Variation 3...Bf5 played by Tal, Larsen, Gheorghiu in the 1980s.
Used by King's Indian players to avoid the Samisch and Averbakh systems.

typical_structures.structure: Philidor-like: Black pawns d6/e5 against White e4/d4 centre, tense; Black slightly cramped, bishops on e7 and c8
Neo-Old Indian / Modern 2...g6: Black fianchetto set-ups resembling the King's Indian or Pirc

character.notes: Rated Balanced sharpness and Easy difficulty by Chessiverse. Considered sound and harder to crack than the King's Indian below master level. Black's position is solid but slightly passive; no forcing main line (Ukrainian main line is slow). Black has few ways to lose quickly, although White keeps a small edge.

gambit.notes: No pawn is given in the main lines.

soundness.notes: Considered sound; Wikipedia says the main line leaves White slightly better. Less active than the King's Indian fianchetto.

structure.notes: Central pawns on d6/e5 vs d4/e4 usually stay on; the centre is closed or tense with White's space advantage (Philidor-like). An early ...exd4 or e5xd4 opening is possible but not typical.

approach.notes: A semi-system: a flexible d6/e5 set-up, often used as an alternative to the King's Indian. Never reached the popularity of the King's Indian. At 2500+ level, 3.Nc3 is played in 61% and 3.Nf3 in 35% of games; theory adherence is high (about 99% of moves follow known lines). Played by strong players (Tal, Larsen, Gheorghiu, Gligoric as White), though rarely a main weapon.

level.notes: Chessiverse rates it Easy. Black needs to understand the cramped Philidor-style structure and the timing of ...c6 and ...a5 plans more than memorising lines, although White's slightly better main line asks for patience. Judged for Black.

sublines_that_differ.name: Neo-Old Indian: Modern (2...g6)
sublines_that_differ.how: Black fianchettoes; transposes to the King's Indian or Pirc-like structures; more dynamic than the e7-bishop set-up.

sublines_that_differ.name: Old Indian: Janowski Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 d6 3. Nc3 Bf5
sublines_that_differ.how: Early bishop development outside the pawn chain; played by Tal, Larsen and Gheorghiu.

sublines_that_differ.name: Old Indian: 3.Nf3
sublines_that_differ.how: White waits with Nc3; Black can choose ...Nbd7 and ...e5 or fianchetto.

description.claim: The Old Indian is a solid and resilient system.
description.note: Called sound and harder to crack than the King's Indian.

description.claim: Black prioritises creating a robust, flexible structure, delaying the development of the king's knight.
description.note: In the standard Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6) Black develops the king's knight at once; Black delays ...Nf6 only in the 1.d4 d6 move order, which usually transposes. The delay is in the bishop (e7, no fianchetto), not the knight.

description.claim: Black prepares the crucial ...e5 pawn break to challenge White's spatial advantage.
description.note: ...e5 is the key move of the structure.

description.claim: Leads to strategically complex games; excellent for patient positional players who are comfortable in slightly cramped quarters.
description.note: Cramped but sound; Philidor-like. Chessiverse rates difficulty Easy.

common_plans.claim: Black: Prepare and execute ...e5 with ...Nbd7, ...Be7 and ...O-O.
White: Use the space advantage to restrict Black and prevent or meet ...e5.
common_plans.note: Main line gives White slight edge.

common_plans.claim: Black: If ...e5 is difficult, shift to the queenside with ...c6 and ...b5.
common_plans.note: ...c6 is a standard move in the main line; ...b5 is not named; other follow-ups are ...a5 and ...Na6.

common_plans.claim: White: Develop to optimal squares (Nf3, Be2, O-O, Nc3) and exploit weaknesses.
common_plans.note: Matches the main line Nf3, Be2, O-O, Nc3, Re1.
